sections.title: Distinguish waiting from lifting operations
paragraphs: An airline catering company transported meal carts between its catering facility and aircraft stands.

Vehicle location alone did not show when lifting operations began, whether the monitored securing condition was present or whether the platform had been lowered before departure. Supervisors also needed temperature records from the catering compartment to review conditions during each service run.

sections.title: Connect lift activity with driver warnings
paragraphs: The pilot equipped 20 high-lift catering trucks. SMART S-4537 collected supported vehicle and high-lift equipment data. One CAN connection supplied chassis information, including mileage, engine RPM, fuel-related readings and vehicle condition. The second supplied available platform-position, lifting and service-door information from the compatible body controller. A Bluetooth temperature sensor monitored the insulated compartment. Separate inputs recorded ignition and the installed wheel-chock or stabilisation signal.

points.title: Review activity at the aircraft stand
points.text: Supervisors could examine vehicle arrival, lifting activity, platform position and departure in the same journey record. This helped distinguish travel, waiting and equipment operation. When servicing was delayed, staff could identify the relevant period and discuss it with the crew. Chassis information added context if a vehicle fault or operating condition required investigation.

points.title: Warn about conflicting operating conditions
points.text: Complex Events evaluated the monitored signals together. Configured conditions could activate an in-cab buzzer—for example, lifting activity without the expected securing signal, or vehicle movement with the platform still raised. The warning prompted the driver to check the situation. It supplemented operating procedures and existing safety systems; it did not independently verify complete vehicle stability or automatically prevent movement.

points.title: Review catering-compartment temperature
points.text: Temperature readings could be examined alongside the journey and servicing activity, giving staff a record of conditions at the sensor location. These readings supported delivery reviews but did not independently establish the temperature or condition of every meal cart.

sections.title: Clearer delay reviews and driver warnings
paragraphs: Supervisors could investigate servicing delays using recorded equipment activity rather than arrival and departure times alone. They could discuss a particular stage of the job with the crew and coordinate the next action.
The configured buzzer drew the driver’s attention to selected operating conflicts during the task. Temperature history also supported subsequent checks of catering transport conditions.

sections.title: Locate delays and prompt operating checks
paragraphs: S-4537 helped supervisors understand where an aircraft-service delay occurred: while the truck was travelling to the stand, waiting to begin work or operating its lift. This gave them a basis for contacting the relevant crew and coordinating the remaining work when timely catering delivery mattered.

The installation also brought warnings directly to the driver when a monitored conflict occurred, such as movement with the platform raised. Recognising the situation and stopping to check could help avoid equipment damage and further disruption to servicing.

For the company, the value was practical oversight of work at the aircraft: investigate a delay, coordinate with the crew and draw attention to an operating error before it caused additional downtime.

sections.title: Check tools returned after a service visit
paragraphs: A telecom maintenance company sent technicians to mobile network sites with network testers, diagnostic kits and specialised tools.

Vehicle tracking showed where the vans travelled, but did not tell the company whether important equipment had returned with the technician after a visit. A forgotten tool could interrupt the next assignment and require a return journey.
The company also needed to identify the technician responsible for each vehicle and service visit.

sections.title: Warn about missing equipment and review stops
paragraphs: The installation covered six service vans. SMART S-2433 trackers were installed in the service vans, and BLE beacons were attached to selected high-value equipment. A Complex Events program was adapted to monitor multiple registered beacons and activate an in-cab buzzer when a configured missing-equipment condition was met. A 1-Wire RFID reader identified the registered technician. Ignition and rear cargo-door signals added context to vehicle stops and equipment access.

points.title: Prompt a check before the next job
points.text: The adapted program monitored the registered equipment tags. If an expected beacon was no longer detected under the configured conditions, the tracker activated the buzzer. The warning prompted the technician to check the equipment rather than discover a missing tester or tool case at the next assignment. Beacon detection indicated proximity to the vehicle; a missing signal prompted verification rather than automatically proving that an item had been lost.

points.title: Identify where to begin the search
points.text: Staff could review the missing-equipment event alongside the preceding service stop, cargo-door activity and registered technician. This helped determine whom to contact and which site to check first. The records supported investigation of where equipment might have been left; they did not continuously track an item once it was beyond the van’s reception range.

sections.title: Equipment checks during the service route
paragraphs: Technicians received an audible prompt when the configured checks identified missing equipment. The operations team could follow up using the relevant vehicle, technician and service-visit records.
This established an equipment-check process during the route, giving staff an opportunity to find an omitted item before it disrupted another job.

sections.title: Keep technicians equipped for the next job
paragraphs: S-2433 helped the company act on a possible equipment omission while the technician was still on the service route. The adapted Complex Events logic brought the issue directly to the cab, while the journey history gave the office a starting point for recovery.

For the maintenance company, the value was keeping technicians equipped to complete their assignments. Checking a missing item sooner could avoid a wasted return journey, a delayed repair or unnecessary replacement of equipment that could still be recovered.

sections.title: Detect a rise from the project’s −18°C setting
paragraphs: A frozen-food distributor operated 34 refrigerated vehicles in Astana. The project’s normal transport temperature was −18°C.

The company needed to know promptly when temperature began to rise, so staff could contact the driver and request a check during the delivery. Monitoring the whole fleet manually made it difficult to identify which vehicle needed attention.

sections.title: Alert at −17°C using individual readings
paragraphs: SMART S-2421 trackers were installed in all 34 vehicles. Each refrigerated compartment had two wired temperature sensors connected through 1-Wire. Alerts were configured through the device’s standard settings, without Complex Events.

points.title: Notify the operator at −17°C
points.text: If either sensor reported a temperature reaching −17°C, the tracker sent an urgent SMS notification to the operator. This was a one-degree rise from the project’s normal temperature of −18°C. The alert used individual sensor readings, so a deviation at one monitored point could trigger a notification without being averaged with the other reading. The threshold was a setting for this project, rather than a universal limit for all frozen products.

points.title: Direct attention to the affected delivery
points.text: The notification allowed the operator to identify the vehicle requiring attention and contact its driver. Staff could request a check of the refrigeration unit and cargo-compartment conditions, then determine the next action from the findings. The temperature alert identified a condition requiring investigation; it did not automatically establish equipment failure or product damage.

sections.title: A consistent alert process across 34 vehicles
paragraphs: The distributor gained a consistent alert process across 34 vehicles. Operators could focus on deliveries where a monitored temperature reached −17°C instead of continuously checking every vehicle’s readings.
This provided an opportunity to investigate a developing temperature problem while the shipment was still in transit.

sections.title: Focus on deliveries needing early attention
paragraphs: S-2421 helped the supplier identify which delivery needed attention as soon as a monitored temperature reached the configured warning level. With 34 vehicles on the road, staff could direct their response to a specific truck rather than rely on routine calls or continuous manual checks.

For the business, the value was the opportunity to act before a temperature deviation continued unnoticed. Timely investigation could help limit deterioration of frozen products, rejected deliveries and replacement costs, without requiring a custom control program for the alert.

sections.title: Know when a deviation starts and ends
paragraphs: A dairy distributor operated 12 refrigerated trucks with ageing refrigeration units. Equipment failures created a risk of rising cargo temperatures during deliveries.

The supplier needed to know when a monitored area became too warm and when its temperature returned to the configured range. Staff could then follow up during the journey instead of discovering a problem only at delivery.

sections.title: Monitor each sensor and report recovery
paragraphs: SMART S-2421 trackers were installed in all 12 trucks. Four wired temperature sensors were connected through 1-Wire in each refrigerated compartment. Temperature notifications were configured using the device’s standard settings, without Complex Events.

points.title: Detect a deviation at an individual sensor
points.text: When any connected sensor reported a temperature above 5°C, the tracker sent an SMS notification to the responsible employee. The rule monitored individual readings rather than their average. A warmer reading at one sensor could therefore trigger an alert even if the other three remained below the threshold. Staff could contact the driver and request a check of the refrigeration equipment and cargo-compartment conditions.

points.title: Receive confirmation of temperature recovery
points.text: The device sent a further SMS when the affected sensor returned to the configured normal range. This helped staff follow the event through to recovery instead of relying only on the initial warning. If a recovery message had not arrived, they had a reason to follow up with the driver. A recovery notification confirmed the temperature reading had returned to range; it did not independently establish the condition of the dairy products.

sections.title: Notifications from deviation to recovery
paragraphs: The supplier gained notifications covering both the start and end of a temperature deviation across its 12 trucks.

Staff could direct attention to an affected vehicle, request a check and see whether the monitored temperature subsequently recovered. This reduced the need to repeatedly request temperature updates from drivers or continuously watch readings.

sections.title: Follow exceptions without a custom program
paragraphs: S-2421 gave the supplier a practical way to manage temperature exceptions across a larger fleet. Staff knew which delivery needed attention and received a follow-up when the affected reading recovered, helping them distinguish an ongoing problem from one that had returned to the configured range.

For a distributor using ageing refrigeration equipment, that meant an opportunity to intervene during transport. Earlier attention could help limit spoilage, rejected deliveries and replacement costs. The required warning-and-recovery process was achieved through standard device settings, without a custom control program.

page.h1: Dairy Temperature Alerts in Istanbul
page.lead: Complex Events calculated the average cargo temperature onboard eight trucks and sent an SMS above 5°C, while an in-cab buzzer warned drivers when the cargo door stayed open for more than five minutes.
page.heroAlt: Illustrative refrigerated dairy delivery truck at a distribution warehouse in Istanbul, Turkey

sections.title: Detect rising temperature during delivery
paragraphs: A dairy distributor operated eight refrigerated trucks with ageing refrigeration units. Equipment failures had occurred, creating a risk of temperature deviations during deliveries.

The company needed timely notification of rising temperatures so staff could contact the driver and arrange a check while the shipment was still in transit. They also needed to know where the truck was and whether the cargo door had been opened.

sections.title: Alert staff to temperature rises and drivers to open doors
paragraphs: SMART S-2433 trackers were installed in the trucks. Each refrigerated compartment had four temperature sensors, one in each corner, connected to the tracker through 1-Wire. A door sensor recorded opening and closing events. Temperature readings, door status and vehicle location were available in the monitoring system.

points.title: Automatically report rising temperature
points.text: An algorithm configured through Complex Events calculated the average of the four temperature readings directly inside the tracker. When the average exceeded 5°C, the device sent an SMS to the responsible employee. Staff could then contact the driver and request a check of the refrigeration equipment and cargo-compartment conditions. The 5°C threshold was the project’s configured alert setting. An average below that threshold did not establish that every individual sensor location was below 5°C.

points.title: Warn the driver when the door stays open
points.text: If the cargo door remained open for more than five minutes, an in-cab buzzer sounded. This prompted the driver to check the door and close it once access was no longer needed, helping avoid unnecessarily prolonged openings. The buzzer was a door-open warning. It did not stop the engine or control the refrigeration unit.

points.title: Review door activity before the next check
points.text: Staff could examine the truck’s location and door events when investigating a temperature rise. This helped establish whether unloading was taking place or whether temperature was increasing with the compartment closed, requiring further investigation of the refrigeration equipment. A door opening provided context rather than automatically proving the cause.

sections.title: Temperature alerts for staff and door warnings for drivers
paragraphs: The distributor received automatic SMS notifications when the average temperature exceeded the configured limit. Staff no longer needed to continuously watch the monitoring screen to detect that condition.

Drivers also received an audible reminder when the cargo door stayed open for more than five minutes, without waiting for a dispatcher to call. Staff could use temperature, door and location history when following up on a delivery.

sections.title: Intervene while products are still in transit
paragraphs: S-2433 gave the supplier an opportunity to intervene while the dairy products were still in transit. Staff could identify the truck needing attention and ask the driver to check the refrigeration equipment before the delivery continued unnoticed under unsuitable conditions.

The door warning brought a separate issue directly to the driver’s attention: access to the cargo compartment remaining open for too long. It gave the person at the vehicle an opportunity to respond without waiting for office intervention.

This was particularly useful with ageing refrigeration units: the supplier could prioritise a vehicle showing a problem without assigning someone to watch every truck throughout the day. Earlier intervention could help limit product spoilage, rejected deliveries and replacement costs, while the journey records supported investigation of recurring refrigeration problems.

paragraphs: A sightseeing-boat operator in Mumbai needed to follow its vessels during passenger trips, review their routes and speeds, and understand how the engines were being operated.
The operator also wanted crews to be able to request assistance with the boat’s location available to the person responding.
Communication was another consideration. The installation needed to make use of available coastal cellular coverage while allowing the tracker to remain in a protected position onboard.

points.title: Review routes, speed and engine operation
points.text: The operator could follow reported boat positions and review completed excursions. Route and speed records helped identify deviations or operating periods that required discussion with the crew. RPM readings added context to those checks. Staff could examine engine speed alongside vessel movement, rather than judging engine operation from the route alone. RPM did not independently establish fuel consumption or engine condition.

points.title: Request assistance with location context
points.text: If help was needed, a crew member could press the connected button. The monitoring system received an assistance event, allowing the operator to identify the boat and review its reported coordinates before contacting the crew and coordinating a response. Delivery of the event depended on available cellular communication. The button complemented onboard emergency procedures rather than replacing marine distress equipment.

points.title: Position antennas for better reception
points.text: External antennas could be placed where surrounding structures caused less obstruction, while the tracker remained protected onboard. Support for 4G and 2G allowed the installation to use an available compatible network. Antenna placement helped make use of existing coverage; it did not provide connectivity beyond cellular service areas.

sections.title: Journey records and crew assistance requests
paragraphs: The operator gained a record of where each boat travelled, its reported speed and the associated engine RPM. This provided a basis for reviewing excursions and following up on particular route or operating events with the crew.
The assistance button also gave crews a direct way to request attention, with the vessel’s reported location available to support the response.

sections.title: Keep vessel activity and requests accessible
paragraphs: S-4753 helped the operator maintain oversight after a boat left the harbour. Staff could review its journey and respond to an assistance request using location information from the same vessel.

page.h1: Paid Generator Rental Periods in Gurugram
page.lead: A 28-generator rental company linked online extension payments with remote equipment restrictions and voltage-based operating-hour records.
page.heroAlt: Illustrative turquoise rental diesel generator installed on a concrete pad at a customer site in Gurugram

sections.title: Restrict unpaid use and review operating time
paragraphs: A generator rental company charged customers by the day and accepted online payments for rental extensions.
The owner needed to prevent continued use when a rental period expired without payment. The company also wanted to know how many hours each generator operated while deployed at a customer site.

sections.title: Link paid rental periods with equipment control
paragraphs: START S-2011 trackers connected the generators to the rental-management system. A connected relay controlled generator operation, while external supply voltage was used to determine engine-running periods and accumulate operating hours.

points.title: Apply the paid rental period
points.text: When a rental expired without a paid extension, the rental system automatically sent a blocking command to the tracker. After receiving it, S-2011 activated the connected relay and stopped the generator’s engine. The rental system checked payment status; the tracker carried out the command at the equipment.

points.title: Restore permission after payment
points.text: Once an online extension payment was confirmed, the system sent an unblocking command. The tracker released the relay restriction, allowing the customer to operate the generator again. Releasing the restriction restored permission to operate; it did not automatically restart the engine.

points.title: Record operating hours
points.text: The installation used external supply-voltage conditions as an indication that the engine was running. The tracker accumulated the time during which those configured conditions were met. These records helped the owner review generator usage and plan servicing. They represented voltage-based operating-hour estimates, rather than readings from the generator’s own hour meter. Daily rental charges remained separate from operating hours.

sections.title: Remote rental control and usage records
paragraphs: The company connected its online rental-extension process to equipment control. An unpaid extension triggered a blocking command, while confirmed payment allowed the restriction to be released remotely.
Staff did not need to visit a site solely to apply or remove the restriction. The owner also gained operating-hour records for reviewing usage across the 28 generators.

sections.title: Act on payment status at customer sites
paragraphs: START S-2011 gave the rental company a way to act on payment status while the generator was already at a customer site. The owner could restrict continued use after an unpaid rental period and restore permission once the extension was paid.

The same installation recorded operating time using the available supply-voltage signal. For this project, the value was practical control over rental use and a basis for maintenance planning, without requiring staff to collect operating-hour readings in person.

sections.title: Check charge readiness and registered drivers
paragraphs: A tourist transport company operated 17 electric buses between Delhi and Jaipur. Each bus needed to be fully charged before its scheduled departure, using the company’s four charging stations across the two cities.

The operator needed to know which buses required charging, which were actually charging and which were ready for assignment. The company also wanted to follow journeys and identify the driver responsible for each shift.

sections.title: Connect charging, journeys and driver records
paragraphs: SMART S-2435 trackers supplied battery charge level, charging status, mileage and location to the monitoring platform. A driver-card reader connected through 1-Wire supported driver identification and shift records.

points.title: Check readiness before assigning a bus
points.text: The operator could compare battery levels and charging status at both locations. This distinguished a bus receiving charge from one simply parked and waiting. Staff could identify vehicles still needing preparation and check that a selected bus was fully charged before assigning it to a departure.

points.title: Receive charging-completion notifications
points.text: The monitoring platform notified the operator when a bus reached 100% charge. Staff could then coordinate its next assignment and arrange for another bus to use the charging station. This replaced repeated checks of charging progress with a notification tied to a clear operational action.

points.title: Follow journeys and review mileage
points.text: Live location updates helped staff follow buses during tourist transfers. Trip history supported checks of departure and arrival times, while mileage records showed the distance travelled. These records helped the operator coordinate vehicles for subsequent journeys.

points.title: Identify drivers and record shifts
points.text: Drivers inserted their personal cards at the start of a shift and kept them in the reader while operating the bus. Card insertion and removal marked the beginning and end of the registered shift. In this installation, card presence was also required for propulsion: removing the card disabled traction, including during movement. This was not an automatic braking function. Card records linked vehicle activity to the registered driver; they did not independently verify who was physically driving throughout the shift.

sections.title: Readiness checks linked to trips and shifts
paragraphs: The operator could review the readiness of all 17 buses across both cities before assigning departures. Charging status showed whether preparation had started, and completion notifications identified buses ready for their next journey.
Location, mileage and driver records supported follow-up on individual trips and registered shifts. Staff had less need to reconstruct vehicle readiness and activity from separate driver updates.

sections.title: Coordinate charging and departures in two cities
paragraphs: S-2435 helped the company answer the question that mattered before each departure: is this bus charged and ready for the next assignment? Staff could distinguish a parked vehicle from one charging and act when charging was complete.

With 17 buses sharing four stations in two cities, this gave the operator a practical basis for coordinating charging and departures. Driver identification added accountability by linking each registered shift to the vehicle’s journey record.

page.h1: Charging Coordination for 14 Buses in Mumbai
page.lead: Battery readings and completion notifications helped an employee transport operator coordinate 14 electric buses sharing two charging stations.
page.note: Mumbai, India · 14 OLECTRA iX buses · Two charging stations
page.heroAlt: Illustrative electric commuter buses connected to two charging stations at a Mumbai depot

sections.title: Prioritise charging before scheduled departures
paragraphs: An employee transport operator in Mumbai had 14 electric buses sharing two charging stations. The dispatcher needed to decide which bus to charge first and when to connect the next vehicle.

Battery checks depended on drivers. The dispatcher had to call them for charge levels and charging progress, and updates were not always timely. When several buses were waiting, it was difficult to prioritise charging around upcoming departures.

sections.title: Use battery readings to coordinate charging
paragraphs: SMART S-2435 trackers collected battery state of charge, state of health, charging status, mileage and available fault information. These readings were displayed in the connected monitoring system.

points.title: Prioritise buses waiting for a charger
points.text: The dispatcher could compare battery percentages across the fleet and see which buses were already charging. Reviewing this information alongside the departure schedule helped determine which bus needed the next available station. Charging decisions no longer depended solely on drivers checking and reporting their battery levels.

points.title: Connect the next bus after charging
points.text: When a bus reached 100% charge, the monitoring platform notified the operator. The operator could then instruct a driver to move the charged bus and connect the next vehicle. This replaced repeated calls and physical checks with a notification that prompted a specific action.

points.title: Check vehicle condition before assignment
points.text: Mileage records supported maintenance scheduling based on actual use. Reported faults helped staff identify buses needing a technical check before assignment. Battery state-of-health readings provided additional context for maintenance assessment, rather than a standalone prediction of battery failure.

sections.title: A clearer charging queue and changeover process
paragraphs: The dispatcher gained a consistent process for managing the charging queue: check battery levels, consider upcoming departures, prioritise waiting buses and arrange a changeover when charging was complete.

Staff no longer needed to repeatedly call drivers or inspect buses to establish charging progress. Completion notifications helped them coordinate the removal of charged vehicles and connection of the next bus.

sections.title: Prepare buses around limited charging capacity

When a bus reached 100%, its reported charge level enabled the monitoring platform to notify the dispatcher. The dispatcher could immediately arrange for the station to be released and the next bus connected, without repeated phone calls or parking-area checks.

sections.title: Link driver access, equipment position and fuel discrepancies
paragraphs: A forestry company operated timber trucks between logging areas, temporary storage yards and processing plants. Supervisors needed to investigate unusual fuel losses and ensure that only authorised drivers could start the vehicles.

sections.title: Separate movement warnings and start control
paragraphs: The pilot equipped 10 timber trucks in Minsk, Belarus. SMART S-4511 trackers collected location and Bluetooth fuel-level readings. Four wired inputs recorded ignition, crane operation, crane-stowed position and stabilizer status. A 1-Wire RFID reader identified the registered driver.

points.title: Warn the driver before the situation continues
points.text: Complex Events combined these signals to control two separate responses: an equipment warning and permission to start the engine. If movement was detected while the crane was not stowed or the stabilizers remained deployed, the tracker recorded an event and activated an in-cab buzzer. The driver could stop and check the equipment, while supervisors could review the event afterwards. This supplemented departure checks; it was not an automatic movement interlock. Crane-operation records also helped distinguish loading activity from other stops on the route.

points.title: Restrict starting to authorised drivers
points.text: The second output controlled a start-blocking relay. A recognised driver card was required before starting was permitted, linking the shift to the registered driver. This restricted unauthorised starts without using the relay to stop an engine already running.

points.title: Investigate fuel changes at a specific stop
points.text: A significant fuel-level drop while the truck was parked with the ignition off was highlighted for investigation. Staff could review the location, time and driver record, then request an explanation or arrange an inspection. A level drop was treated as a discrepancy to check, rather than automatic proof of theft. On routes with mixed coverage, the tracker could use a supported 2G network when LTE was unavailable. Live updates still depended on cellular coverage.

sections.title: Authorised starts and targeted follow-up
paragraphs: Starting permission was linked to a recognised driver card, and drivers received a warning when movement coincided with deployed equipment.
Supervisors could investigate an unusual fuel drop against the stop and registered driver. This gave them a particular event to discuss instead of a general concern about missing fuel.

sections.title: Warn drivers and control starting
paragraphs: S-4511 let the company apply driver authorisation before starting and warn the driver when movement conflicted with the crane or stabilizer position. These actions did not require a supervisor to watch every departure.

Pump operation alone was not treated as proof of a completed delivery.

points.title: Investigate interrupted unloading
points.text: If the pump was running and the valve was open but little or no flow was recorded, staff could ask the driver to check the unloading process. The combined record helped distinguish an equipment check from a delivery that was still progressing normally. A low-flow event prompted investigation; it did not identify a blockage or other cause by itself.

points.title: Warn about an open valve during movement
points.text: A buzzer connected to a tracker output warned the driver if the tanker began moving while the outlet valve remained open. The warning prompted a stop and valve check; it did not automatically prevent movement.

sections.title: Check reported deliveries against discharge
paragraphs: Staff could compare the reported delivery with the recorded quantity and temperature at the customer’s stop.

sections.title: Make every discharge accountable

sections.title: Check fuel receipts against events along each route
paragraphs: The company delivered food from its central warehouse to retail stores in different cities. Fuel receipts showed what drivers purchased, but did not show how the fuel level changed throughout each delivery.

The fleet manager needed to check whether recorded purchases corresponded with refuelling events and identify unexpected drops requiring investigation. Relying on receipts and driver reports alone made it difficult to establish when and where a discrepancy occurred.

sections.title: Link fuel readings, location and ignition
paragraphs: The company’s 17 delivery trucks were equipped with START S-2013 trackers and wired fuel-level sensors connected through RS-485. Ignition signals were also connected to provide additional context for reviewing fuel events.

points.title: Checking refuelling against receipts
points.text: The monitoring platform brought fuel-level readings together with vehicle location and time. Fleet staff could identify recorded increases in tank level and compare those events with submitted receipts. This gave the manager a way to check whether the time and location of a reported purchase matched the vehicle’s fuel record and investigate discrepancies with the driver.

points.title: Investigating unexpected fuel drops
points.text: Fuel history could be reviewed alongside trips and stops. When an unexpected drop appeared during a stop, staff could locate the event and examine the readings before and after it. This helped narrow an investigation to a specific part of the delivery route. Unusual changes were treated as events to check, rather than automatic proof of fuel theft.

points.title: Adding ignition context
points.text: Ignition status helped staff distinguish fuel events recorded with the ignition on from those recorded with it off. Together with movement and fuel history, this provided a clearer sequence of events. Ignition status was used as context; it did not independently confirm that the engine was running.

sections.title: Traceable fuel events for follow-up
paragraphs: The distributor could check fuel receipts against recorded refuelling on its 17 trucks.

In one customer-reported check, the receipt and sensor-based refuelling estimate differed by 10 litres. This gave staff a specific event to investigate with the driver, rather than an unexplained difference in the overall fuel bill.

sections.title: Check receipts against refuelling records

sections.title: Distinguish travel, waiting and recorded crane activity
paragraphs: The company deployed mobile cranes across construction and industrial projects. The owner needed to know where each crane was and whether it was travelling, waiting on site or performing work.

Location and engine-running status alone could not answer these questions. A crane could remain on a project site with its engine running without carrying out lifting operations. This made it difficult to assess equipment utilisation and investigate extended waiting periods.

sections.title: Link chassis, crane activity and communication
paragraphs: SIGNAL S-4753 terminals were installed on 5 mobile cranes and connected to the chassis and compatible crane-control systems.

points.title: Separate travel, waiting and crane activity
points.text: One CAN connection collected supported chassis parameters, including mileage, engine hours, RPM and coolant temperature. The second connection collected available operating states from the crane-control system. Additional inputs monitored approved signals, including PTO operation and outrigger status, where these were unavailable through CAN. The monitoring platform brought these records together with location and movement data. Dispatchers could distinguish travel from time on site and review recorded crane-equipment activity. When a crane remained on site without working events, the dispatcher could contact the operator to establish the reason: restricted site access, a load that was not ready or a change in the assignment. This gave the team a practical basis for adjusting schedules and allocating equipment between projects.

points.title: Additional operator warnings
points.text: Terminal outputs controlled approved in-cabin buzzers or warning indicators. When a configured condition occurred, the operator received a signal prompting attention and a check. Crane operating events could also be reviewed alongside PTO and outrigger states to investigate the sequence of operations. These warnings supplemented the crane’s original safety systems. They did not replace its protective interlocks or determine whether a lift was safe from an outrigger-status signal alone.

points.title: Direct communication with the control room
points.text: Two-way voice communication allowed operators to discuss breakdowns, route changes and site instructions through the installed equipment. The dispatcher could review the crane’s location and available operating data during the conversation. This provided context for troubleshooting and coordination without relying solely on the operator’s personal phone.

points.title: Maintenance planning based on actual use
points.text: The maintenance team could review mileage, engine hours and crane operating states together. This helped account for work performed on site that would not appear in mileage records and supported servicing according to the relevant maintenance schedules. Coolant-temperature data provided additional context when investigating abnormal engine operation.

sections.title: Discuss delays and plan the next job
paragraphs: Dispatch could examine travel, waiting and recorded crane activity before discussing an assignment or delay with the operator.
Direct voice contact supported coordination during problems. Maintenance staff could also consider crane activity alongside engine use when planning service.

sections.title: Understand what the hired crane is doing on site
paragraphs: S-4753 helped the rental company distinguish travel, waiting and recorded crane work, giving dispatch a basis for discussing delays and the next assignment with the operator. Maintenance could also consider lifting-equipment activity alongside engine use.

Direct voice contact supported that discussion during a problem. The owner gained a way to coordinate equipment already at a customer site instead of treating arrival as evidence that useful work had begun.

sections.title: Move beyond an isolated temperature alert
paragraphs: The company transported food between a central cold-storage facility, supermarkets and regional distribution points.

Temperature monitoring could identify an excursion, but an alert alone did not explain what required attention. Staff needed to establish whether the refrigeration unit was operating, whether its temperature setting was appropriate or whether a door had remained open during unloading.

Without that context, the dispatcher had to contact the driver and reconstruct the situation before deciding what to check. The company needed temperature readings and equipment status connected to the same delivery record.

sections.title: Link temperature, controller and door records
paragraphs: The company equipped 9 refrigerated trucks with SMART S-4533 trackers, connecting cargo temperatures, refrigeration-controller data, door events and vehicle location in the monitoring platform.

points.title: Monitor conditions across the cargo compartment
points.text: Temperature sensors monitored different areas of the refrigerated compartment. Their readings provided a history of conditions at the monitored locations throughout the journey. The dispatcher could review temperature changes alongside the truck’s position and delivery stops, helping identify when and where an excursion developed.

points.title: Check what the refrigeration unit was doing
points.text: The refrigeration controller was connected through RS-485 using Modbus. The integration collected supported parameters, including operating status, set temperature, runtime and available alarm conditions. This gave staff information beyond the temperature inside the truck. They could check whether the unit reported that it was running, what temperature it was set to maintain and whether it had reported an abnormal condition. The available readings depended on the connected controller and its supported parameters.

points.title: Put door activity alongside temperature changes
points.text: Connected door sensors recorded opening and closing events during loading and unloading. When temperature moved outside the permitted range, the dispatcher could check whether the change coincided with a door opening, how long the door remained open and what the refrigeration unit reported during that period. These records helped distinguish circumstances requiring different responses. A prolonged door opening prompted a check with the driver; a controller alarm directed attention to the refrigeration equipment.

points.title: Respond with a specific check
points.text: Staff reviewed the combined records before contacting the driver. Instead of reporting only that the cargo compartment was too warm, they could ask the driver to check an open door, confirm the controller setting or investigate a reported alarm. The information helped narrow the investigation. It did not automatically establish the cause of every excursion or replace inspection of the equipment and affected goods.

sections.title: Target door, setting and alarm checks
paragraphs: Staff could review unloading activity and refrigeration reports before contacting the driver about a temperature deviation.
The combined history supported a targeted check during the journey and later review of the delivery, without automatically declaring a cause for the deviation.

sections.title: Guide checks after a temperature alert
paragraphs: S-4533 let the dispatcher examine what the refrigeration equipment reported when cargo temperature changed. That helped staff choose between checking an open door, a temperature setting or a reported equipment alarm before contacting the driver.
For the distributor, the value was a more informed response during delivery and a record for reviewing the handover. A temperature alert became the start of a targeted investigation.

paragraphs: START S-2011 trackers provided location and journey records across the fleet. The operator used this information to review activity by bike and rental location, then make decisions about rotation and servicing.

points.text: Tracked mileage helped the operator identify bikes approaching their maintenance intervals and arrange servicing before allocating further rentals. sections.title: Balanced use and predictable servicing

page.lead: A scooter rental operator used Navtelecom SMART S-2421 to locate its fleet, warn riders approaching the permitted boundary and automatically respond when scooters left the rental area.

sections.title: Remind riders before they leave the rental area
paragraphs: The owner rented out 11 scooters on the condition that customers kept them within North Goa. Journeys beyond this area made collection and assistance more difficult.

Explaining the restriction at handover did not allow the owner to monitor compliance during a rental. Customers could overlook the boundary or continue beyond it, while the operator needed to know where the scooter was and respond.

sections.title: Locate, warn and delay blocking by speed
paragraphs: SMART S-2421 trackers connected the scooters to a monitoring platform. One output controlled the warning buzzer, and a separate output controlled the blocking relay. The platform handled geographic boundary checks, while the tracker applied the configured speed condition before blocking.

points.title: Locate scooters during rentals
points.text: The trackers supplied location updates to the platform, allowing the owner to check each scooter’s latest reported position.

points.title: Warn riders before they cross the boundary
points.text: The platform used a warning area approximately 500 metres before the configured outer boundary. When a scooter entered this area, the system triggered a connected buzzer. Customers were informed of the rental restriction and the meaning of the audible warning. The signal reminded them to change direction and remain within the permitted area before a blocking request became necessary.

points.title: Delay blocking until the speed condition is met
points.text: If a scooter left the permitted area, the monitoring platform automatically sent a blocking command to SMART S-2421. The tracker did not activate the blocking relay immediately after receiving the command. It waited until reported speed fell below 15 km/h. This was the project’s activation condition, not an automatic braking command or a guarantee of safety in every riding situation. This created a staged response: an audible reminder near the boundary, followed by a blocking request after departure, with relay activation controlled by the device’s speed condition. Boundary detection and command delivery depended on location updates and communication with the platform.

sections.title: Better control of the rental service territory
paragraphs: The customer reported more manageable collection and assistance across its 11-scooter fleet.
Location records helped the owner find scooters, while the boundary warning reminded renters to turn back. Departures could be handled through the configured speed-conditioned blocking process.

sections.title: Warn renters before boundary crossings
paragraphs: S-2421 brought the service-area restriction to the rider through an audible reminder near the boundary. If the scooter left the area, the configured blocking request was subject to the device’s speed condition.

This supported the owner’s aim of keeping the 11 scooters within a manageable collection and assistance area. Location reporting helped find the scooter when intervention was needed; the warning gave the renter a chance to turn back first.

points.text: S-4533 collected charge and available battery-condition data from the battery management system and transmitted them alongside the scooter’s location. When the scooter left the restricted zone, the server automatically sent an updated command through the same path. The scooter switched to the mode permitted in the next area, restoring the normal operating limit where no additional restriction applied. paragraphs: The operator could locate its 212 scooters and use battery-charge records to plan collection and charging.

sections.title: Apply riding rules automatically
paragraphs: S-4533 connected the rental service’s decisions to the scooter. The server could request the appropriate riding mode when a scooter entered or left a zone, and the installed logic passed that request to the scooter electronics for gradual application.

page.h1: Irrigation: 18% Lower Reported Water Use
page.lead: Irrigation across 700 hectares was automated using two SMART S-2433 controllers, 32 wired soil sensors and local logic built with Complex Events.
page.note: A tomato farmer replaced routine manual irrigation starts with soil-moisture-based control. Over nine months, the farmer reported 18% less water use. The system operated locally, without an internet connection or monitoring platform, while SMS alerts directed attention to critical soil conditions.
page.heroAlt: Documentary-style scene of sprinkler irrigation among uneven tomato rows, with soil monitoring equipment and a weathered control cabinet

sections.title: Water when the soil needs it — not when someone is available
paragraphs: Manual checks took time and gave the farmer an incomplete picture of moisture below the soil surface. Irrigation depended on someone inspecting conditions and starting the system. That made it difficult to respond consistently as soil dried, while unnecessary watering consumed water and pumping energy.

The farmer needed watering to start when the monitored soil required it and a clear alert when conditions needed inspection. Internet access and a hosted monitoring service were not prerequisites the farm could rely on.

sections.title: Soil readings → local decision → timed watering

points.title: Read the soil. Average each sensor group.
points.text: Each S-2433 acted as a stationary controller connected to 16 wired Modbus RTU sensors. The installation read soil moisture and electrical conductivity (EC) from each sensor. Complex Events processed the readings locally and calculated the average for each controller’s sensor group. The 32 sensors provided sampling points on the 700-hectare farm. Group averages guided the associated irrigation areas; they did not establish uniform moisture across every hectare. Individual dry patches still required field inspection and representative sensor placement.

points.title: Start watering when the soil dries
points.text: When average moisture reached the configured 40% start threshold as the soil dried, the controller activated its output and the relay connected to the sprinkler system’s control circuit. The farmer no longer had to attend each routine irrigation start. The relay controlled the irrigation control circuit, not the pump’s power circuit directly.

points.title: End the cycle after 15 minutes
points.text: After 15 minutes, the controller deactivated the output, ending the watering cycle. Moisture readings continued to be checked. The project used a 40% start threshold and a 30% critical alert threshold on its configured moisture scale. These are installation settings, not general recommendations for tomato irrigation. Their meaning depends on the sensor calibration and soil conditions.

points.title: Keep the control decision local
points.text: Reading sensors, applying the rules and controlling irrigation took place inside the devices. Loss of cellular coverage did not remove the need-based control logic. SMS delivery still depended on cellular service, and local control still required power, working sensors and a functioning irrigation system.

sections.eyebrow: ALERTS THAT LEAD TO A DEFINED ACTION
sections.title: Know when to inspect — and what to check

points.title: Critical drying
points.text: If average moisture fell below the 30% critical setting, the controller generated an SMS. The farmer checked water availability, the irrigation equipment and the soil readings. The alert identified a moisture problem; it did not diagnose a failed pump or confirm that water had flowed.

points.title: Changes in soil conductivity
points.text: Two configured lower EC thresholds generated warning and priority alerts. These prompted review of recent irrigation, sensor condition and soil conditions, with sampling or agronomic advice before changing fertilizer application. EC reflects soluble salts and is also influenced by moisture and temperature; a low reading alone does not establish nutrient deficiency.

sections.title: 18% less water use, reported by the farmer
paragraphs: WATER CONSUMPTION

points.title: 18% reduction
points.text: Water use fell to 82% of the comparison baseline. The farmer reported this reduction over nine months of operation. ELECTRICITY

points.title: Lower use reported
points.text: The farmer also reported lower electricity use. Pumping-energy savings were not quantified and should not be equated with the water-saving percentage. ROUTINE STARTS

points.title: Automated locally
points.text: Less reliance on routine manual irrigation starts. The farmer could focus field visits on moisture and EC alerts instead of attending each routine irrigation start.

points.title: How to interpret these results
points.text: The 18% figure is the farmer’s reported outcome. Baseline water volumes and adjustments for rainfall, crop stage and irrigated area were not supplied. It is not presented as a controlled measurement of the automation’s isolated effect or extrapolated into annual savings.

sections.title: Water when needed without attending every start
paragraphs: S-2433 let the farmer turn soil readings into a watering cycle without travelling to the equipment to start it. The cycle ended after the configured time, and alerts directed attention to conditions needing a field check.

This suited a farm that could not depend on internet access for routine control. The watering decision stayed at the installation, while the farmer could focus on exceptions instead of approving every cycle.

page.h1: Engine Warnings and Fuel Use During Paving Delays
page.lead: Connect engine warnings to maintenance action and identify the diesel used during confirmed paving delays — with SMART S-4535 and a configured monitoring platform.
page.heroAlt: Green tracked asphalt paver and paving crew working on a road in India

sections.title: Keep the paving operation moving
paragraphs: Engine problems interrupt a coordinated work sequence. Delivery gaps can consume diesel even when no asphalt is being laid.

An asphalt paver works as part of a coordinated operation involving the mixing plant, delivery trucks, paving crew and rollers. An engine problem can interrupt that sequence, leaving the crew and arriving material waiting while the maintenance team determines what happened.

The contractor needed engine warnings to reach the responsible supervisor with enough context to organise a response. A telephone report that the machine had stopped did not necessarily explain whether coolant temperature had risen, a warning had escalated or a fault had appeared under load.

Fuel was another concern. The engine could remain running while the paver waited for asphalt deliveries or site preparation. A daily fuel total could not show how much was used during these delays. At the same time, slow movement or low engine load did not automatically mean wasted time: paving, preparation and necessary equipment operation had to be distinguished from avoidable waiting.

sections.title: From a machine event to a site decision

points.title: Respond to an engine warning
points.text: Review supported temperature, speed, load and warning records with time and location. Notify the supervisor and maintenance team with useful context. The operator must follow the manufacturer’s warning and stop procedures. Remote monitoring does not replace the dashboard or delay the required response. SMART S-4535 collects the supported engine coolant temperature, engine speed, load, warning states and diagnostic information from the paver. The configured platform places these readings alongside the time and machine location, and routes relevant notifications to the site supervisor and maintenance team. A sustained temperature excursion or warning prompts the operator to check the machine and follow the manufacturer's operating instructions. The technician can review the conditions leading up to the event and prepare the appropriate inspection. A red stop warning requires the manufacturer's prescribed response; remote monitoring does not replace the operator's dashboard or delay that response. The integrator verifies the available readings on the actual paver before enabling alerts. Warning states guide inspection; identifying the failed component still requires the correct service information.

points.title: Find fuel-consuming delays
points.text: Estimate fuel use from valid fuel-rate readings during confirmed waiting periods, then connect each delay to its recorded cause. Stationary time is not automatically waste. The supervisor confirms the work status; missing readings are not treated as zero consumption. The device also supplies engine-running status and instantaneous fuel rate. The platform can estimate fuel used over a recorded period by integrating valid fuel-rate readings over time. Missing data is flagged rather than silently treated as zero consumption. The supervisor marks the reason for a delay, such as waiting for mix, preparing the work area or an equipment check. Engine speed and load help review the operating conditions, but they do not prove whether asphalt was being laid. Confirmed waiting periods can then be compared with the fuel used during them. If waiting repeatedly coincides with gaps between asphalt deliveries, the supervisor coordinates truck arrivals with the mixing plant and paving crew. sections.title: Where did the diesel go?
paragraphs: A Kumasi logistics company used 55 trucks to move bagged cocoa between buying points, warehouses and processing facilities. Fuel receipts showed what was purchased, but not whether it reached the tank or why one journey used more diesel than another.
Long engine-on waits, unexplained fuel drops and unnecessary empty journeys added to costs. Managers needed to connect each fuel event to a truck, location and assignment, then decide what to change.

points.text: START S-2011 trackers and calibrated Bluetooth fuel level sensors brought tank readings and vehicle positions into one platform. Staff compared refuelling increases with receipts, locations and times. An unusual sustained drop triggered a check with the driver and a review of transfers and surrounding readings. The finding determined the response: correct a record, inspect the installation, check for a leak or investigate suspected draining. A fluctuation alone was not proof of theft.

points.title: Find trips using more fuel than comparable work
points.text: Tank balances and tracked distance supported fuel-use comparisons across similar routes, loads and vehicle classes. Repeatedly high consumption prompted a review of extra distance and operating conditions, followed by a vehicle inspection where needed.

points.title: Reduce avoidable engine-on waiting
points.text: Stationary time, ignition and a validated engine-running indication identified prolonged engine-on waits. A separate input recorded whether air conditioning was on. Necessary operation and cab-cooling needs were considered. Follow-up reports tracked engine-on minutes and overall fuel use.

points.title: Plan collection before dispatch

Repeated delays led to checks that loads were ready and receiving windows agreed. sections.title: Find where the fleet wastes fuel
paragraphs: A construction-materials carrier operates 33 trucks between suppliers, loading yards and customer sites. The fleet faces a recurring problem: engines keep running while trucks wait for loading instructions, access to a site or an available unloading area. On the road, repeated hard acceleration, late braking and excessive speed add another source of avoidable consumption. These losses accumulate across the fleet.

The fleet manager can see the fuel bill and completed trips, but cannot reliably separate fuel used to move a load from fuel burned during unnecessary waiting. Asking every driver to “use less fuel” gives them no specific behaviour to change. Blaming drivers also misses delays caused by dispatching several trucks to the same loading point at once.
The business needs to address both unnecessary engine running and inefficient driving across all 33 trucks, while accounting for routes, loads and working conditions.
Which recurring waits waste diesel?
Which driving habits waste fuel on the road?
Should the driver, dispatcher or site supervisor respond?
Does equivalent work require fewer litres after the change?

sections.title: Reduce waste while waiting and driving
paragraphs: The solution combines S-4535 vehicle data with trip and stop reports in the monitoring platform. Engine-running status, speed and location identify stationary periods with the engine on. Supported fuel-consumption readings help quantify the litres burned during these periods. The integrator verifies the available readings on each vehicle variant and configures the reports before rollout.

points.title: Find where the expense repeats
points.text: The fleet manager reviews engine-on stops by vehicle, location and time of day. Repeated waits at the same loading yard point to a scheduling issue; avoidable running during breaks points to a driver practice. Site records or a verified equipment-status signal distinguish useful stationary work from unnecessary idling.

points.title: Give each problem an owner
points.text: Dispatch staggers arrivals where loading capacity allows. Site supervisors coordinate access and unloading readiness. Drivers switch off during suitable waits under an agreed operating procedure. Equipment operation, regeneration and situations requiring the engine to run are excluded.

points.title: Coach smoother driving with Eco-driving
points.text: The integrator configures acceleration and braking event thresholds for the trucks and validates them on representative trips. The platform combines these events with speed records to flag repeated hard acceleration, harsh braking and speeding against configured limits. The supervisor reviews the trip context with the driver and coaches smoother acceleration, earlier anticipation of stops and steady, appropriate speeds. Necessary emergency braking is not treated as poor driving.

points.title: Verify the effect
points.text: Weekly reviews compare avoidable engine-on time, driving events per 100 km and fuel per 100 km on comparable routes and loads. Fewer events indicate a behaviour change; reduced measured fuel use establishes the saving. Idling and moving fuel are tracked separately. Stop and driving data → recurring waste and inefficient habits → dispatch changes and targeted coaching → fewer litres for the same workload.

page.h1:
Know the trailer.
Account for the fuel.
page.lead: Identify the working tractor–trailer combination and reconcile engine fuel consumption with changes in the tank.
page.heroAlt: CLAAS AXION tractor towing an agricultural roll-off container trailer in a rural setting

sections.title: Two questions dispatch could not answer from position alone

points.title: Which trailer is working?
points.text: The project covered 6 CLAAS AXION 940 tractors and 14 hook-lift trailers. Tractor positions alone did not show which trailer was travelling with each vehicle. When equipment changed between jobs, dispatch had to confirm the combination before assigning the next collection. An unnecessary return to the yard could add distance even when a suitable pickup was ready nearby.

points.title: Where did the diesel go?
points.text: Fuel receipts and tank levels left another question unanswered: how much of the fuel removed from the tank had actually been used by the engine? Without comparing the two, unusually high consumption, a recording error and a possible loss could be difficult to distinguish.

sections.title: Identify. Assign. Reconcile.
paragraphs: SMART S-4535 brings trailer identification, CAN fuel data and Bluetooth tank readings into the same tractor record.

points.title: Identify
points.text: See the working tractor–trailer combination alongside its location and assignment. Each trailer carried an iBeacon tag, while S-4535 was installed on the tractor. The project used Complex Events to process tag information and establish the tractor–trailer association for reporting to the monitoring platform. Dispatch could see the identified combination alongside the tractor’s position and assignment. The internal identification algorithm is not described here. The association identified the tagged trailer; it did not identify an untagged roll-off container carried on it. Container readiness, loading and delivery confirmation remained part of dispatch records. Installation checks needed to distinguish the working trailer from other tagged equipment nearby; receiving a beacon signal alone was not proof of mechanical coupling.

points.title: Dispatch
points.text: Send a suitable, ready combination directly to the next farm when a yard return is not needed. Dispatch used the identified trailer, current location and confirmed job status to select the next collection. When the trailer was suitable, the pickup was ready and no equipment change or empty-container delivery was needed, the tractor could go directly to the next farm instead of returning to the yard.

points.title: Reconcile
points.text: Compare engine-reported consumption with independent tank readings over the same period. S-4535 collected engine-reported fuel consumption through CAN. A calibrated Bluetooth fuel level sensor recorded fuel remaining in the tractor’s tank and the changes associated with refuelling or possible draining. The monitoring platform compared these sources over matching periods and linked exceptions to location and time. Complex Events processes iBeacon information and implements the project’s trailer-association logic. Assignments and fuel exception reports are handled by the monitoring platform.

sections.title: What should remain in the tank?
paragraphs: Compare the expected closing balance with a stable tank reading. Investigate a discrepancy outside the agreed measurement tolerance.
CLIENT-CONFIRMED FUEL CHECK · LITRES
Opening fuel 200
+ Refuelling 150
− Engine use 123
= Expected closing 227
Client-confirmed fuel check. A discrepancy is a reason to investigate — not proof of theft.
Expected closing fuel = opening fuel + recorded refuelling − engine-reported consumption − documented fuel transfers out.

Staff compared this expected balance with the measured closing tank volume. A shortfall outside the agreed measurement tolerance prompted a review of refuelling records, authorised transfers, sensor readings and the journey. Depending on the finding, the next action was to correct a record, inspect a leak or investigate suspected draining.

In the client-confirmed fuel check, the opening balance was 200 litres, refuelling added 150 litres and the engine used 123 litres. The expected closing balance was therefore 227 litres. Against the reported measured balance of 215 litres, this left 12 litres to reconcile before accounting for measurement uncertainty and any documented transfers. The discrepancy was a reason to investigate, not proof that 12 litres had been stolen.

Calibration, aligned reporting periods and reliable CAN readings matter. The comparison helps expose unexplained losses; it does not guarantee that every small loss will be detected or establish theft on its own.
